literature.data: GDE/habitat layers, species maps, greenness & groundwater depth
literature.process: Spatial overlay / suitability scoring; greenness-vs-depth regression
literature.metric: Habitat acreage/quality, focal-species targets, per-GDE threshold
literature.state_text: Outcome quantified. The reviewed literature quantifies habitat and GDE outcomes with reproducible spatial methods, though all four papers are planning or monitoring frameworks rather than operating crediting programs.

detail.data: Howard et al. (2023): DWR NCCAG GDE polygons, USDA Cropland Data Layer, the Chaplin-Kramer et al. (2011) pollinator crop-dependence inventory and USGS National Hydrography Dataset. Bryant et al. (2020): SWAP-projected land retirement plus Stewart et al. (2019) habitat-quality maps for five focal species. Dybala et al. (2025): 30 m 2018 baseline land cover and boosted-regression-tree distribution models for 9 riparian landbird species and 6 waterbird groups. Rohde et al. (2024): Landsat dry-season NDVI (1985–2022) from TNC GDE Pulse for 246,017 NCCAG polygons, paired with CASGEM wells within 250 m.
detail.process: Four approaches. (1) Spatial overlay (Howard): pollinator-dependent cropland within 1 km foraging distance of GDE habitat is summed per basin and normalized by all pollinator-dependent cropland in the basin. (2) Systematic conservation planning (Bryant): prioritizr spatial optimization picks restoration areas that meet habitat targets for five focal species at least agricultural opportunity cost. (3) Land-cover scoring (Dybala): species-distribution models are run on baseline and alternative landscapes; landscape score = Σ(per-ha metric × area of each land-cover class), net effect = alternative minus baseline, with bootstrap uncertainty. (4) Greenness-vs-depth regression (Rohde): NDVI and depth-to-groundwater are standardized to Z-scores per polygon; where the regression slope is significantly negative (p ≤ 0.05), the ZDTG value at ZNDVI = −1 is the local adverse-impact threshold (statewide conservative value ZDTG ≈ 1.3, ~4.0 m). Polygons without wells are scored by the share of drought years with ZNDVI ≥ 0 (drought refugia).
detail.metric: Pollinator-support cropland share; focal-species habitat targets met and the opportunity cost of meeting them; net change in bird habitat/biodiversity support; per-GDE groundwater-depth threshold and annual adverse-impact status; drought-refugia likelihood.
detail.decision: Howard, Bryant and Dybala inform siting, prioritization and scenario comparison (stage: siting → projected outcome). Rohde supports a baseline → annual outcome-monitoring loop that a GSA could run with existing data.
detail.gaps: No paper describes an operational crediting program. Howard's results are an upper bound and do not isolate what GDEs add relative to non-GDE land. Bryant flags additionality and leakage as unresolved before co-benefits can be tied to incentives. Dybala is prospective and does not verify delivered benefits. Rohde notes groundwater data exist for only 1.3% of mapped GDE polygons and NDVI misses slower community-level change. To credit a repurposing project, any of these methods would need a project-vs-counterfactual comparison.

literature.sources: Howard et al. (2023); Bryant et al. (2020); Dybala et al. (2025); Rohde et al. (2024). Method details are from the Literature Evidence sheet of MLRP_Beyond_Water_Savings_Matrix.xlsx. Full citations are in the References block below.

east-turlock.data: Annual photo log; Vegetation/Habitat Quick Assessment
east-turlock.process: Landowner submits form/photos; agency checks completeness
east-turlock.metric: Cover bin %, dominant species (noting native vs. invasive, visual survival percentages
east-turlock.state_text: Practice monitored. ETSGSA has a repeatable vegetation/habitat form and photo log, but it tracks practice persistence with ordinal visual estimates. No threshold or outcome is attached.

detail.data: Annual photo-point log and the Vegetation/Habitat Quick Assessment form (Implementation Monitoring Plan) (ID 136). The practice menu includes Orchard Swale Rewilding, Floodplain Reconnection and Floodflow Spreading (ID 125). Rewilding obligations come from the Incentive Payment Procedures (ID 138).
detail.process: Monitoring has three tiers: (1) the Implementation Monitoring Plan applies to every MLRP project; (2) five practice-specific Implementation Standards add requirements; (3) a Project-Specific Monitoring Checklist, attached to each incentive agreement, selects the add-ons that apply (ID 326). The landowner is the ‘Project Lead Monitor’ and collects photos and completes short forms at each monitoring event. ETSGSA coordinates photo-point locations, receives submissions, performs data checks and aggregates results for DOC reporting. There is no independent field verification (ID 327). The Quick Assessment records cover as a four-bin visual estimate (<25%, 25–50%, 50–75%, >75%), up to five dominant species (noting natives vs. invasives) and a visual percent survival of installed plants. It is an optional per-project add-on, even for Rewilding (ID 136). The Rewilding obligation is to establish and maintain beneficial vegetation from a commercial seed mix for at least 10 years (ID 138).
detail.metric: Cover bin; dominant-species list; visual survival percentage; free-text habitat notes. No threshold attaches to any value (ID 136).
detail.decision: Confirms that the practice was implemented and persists; no ecological result triggers payment, management change or a success determination. The habitat obligation is priced, not measured: Rewilding and Extended Fallowing carry identical water obligations, so the $410/ac/yr rate difference is the price of the habitat obligation (ID 138). Stage: implementation / monitoring.
detail.gaps: No ecological outcome threshold or decision rule. Connectivity/GDE function is not measured. Records are landowner-produced (ID 327). At planning scale, Appendix K states that recharge from rewilding, floodplain reconnection and flood-flow practices ‘has not yet been estimated’ (ID 159). The Implementation Monitoring Plan reviewed is marked DRAFT 12/02/2025 (ID 327 notes). Open: What ecological result would cause ETSGSA to change management, withhold payment or call a habitat project successful?

east-turlock.sources: Phase 2 IDs 125 (ETSGSA MLRP 2026 Application); 136, 326, 327 (ETSGSA MLRP Implementation Monitoring Plan, Vegetation/Habitat Quick Assessment, PDF 5; Roles & Responsibilities); 138 (ETSGSA MLRP Incentive Payment Procedures, Table 1, p. 6); 159 (Turlock GSP Appendix K, §5.1.1, p. 28).

kaweah.data: Flying Dragon project description; no ecological monitoring dataset
kaweah.process: Name habitat as project benefit; conservation easement preserves land use
kaweah.state_text: Named. Habitat is stated as a benefit of specific projects. No GSA in the subbasin scores, measures or monitors it.

detail.data: Project descriptions only: the Flying Dragon Recharge Basin description in EKGSA's 2024 stakeholder outreach report (ID 594), and conditional project language in the MKGSA 2nd Amended GSP (ID 615). No ecological monitoring dataset exists (ID 616).
detail.process: Habitat is named as a project benefit. Flying Dragon (EKGSA; land purchase completed) is described as providing 1,000 AF of recharge, ‘environmental habitat’ and recreation through a conservation easement area on about 58 acres near Seville (IDs 594, 595). The conservation easement is a durability instrument: it locks the land use but does not measure an ecological outcome (ID 615 notes). MKGSA recharge-basin projects ‘would also be combined with other potential project benefits such as habitat restoration’, with no quantity attached (ID 615). A word-boundary search of 12,984 pages found no co-benefit monitoring protocol, habitat form, vegetation assessment or ecological reporting requirement for any repurposing or recharge project in any of the three GSAs (ID 616).
detail.metric: None. Habitat benefit stated qualitatively. The 1,000 AF figure is a recharge design yield, not a habitat metric (ID 594 notes).
detail.decision: Supports project rationale and land acquisition. Stage: siting / implementation.
detail.gaps: Clean absence across EKGSA, GKGSA and MKGSA: no scoring rubric, differentiated rate, monitoring protocol, ecological threshold or DAC screen (ID 615). The best-described project appears in a GSA newsletter-style report, not a plan (ID 594 notes). Open: What minimum ecological monitoring could realistically be sustained on acquired habitat land?

kaweah.sources: Phase 2 IDs 594, 595 (EKGSA 2024 Annual Report – Stakeholder Outreach & Engagement, PDF 8); 615 (Kaweah MKGSA 2nd Amended GSP, Nov 2024, Sec. 6.6.17.1, PDF 381 and Sec. 6.6.18.1, PDF 383); 616 (same GSP set, co-benefit monitoring search).

merced.data: MLRP rubric; wetland designation; connectivity/GDE checkboxes
merced.process: Score ecological benefits at application; verify wetland acreage
merced.state_text: Screened / scored. Ecological benefits are scored once at application. A separate Managed Wetland rule quantifies water for habitat, not habitat condition.

detail.data: MLRP RFP and Application scoring rubric, including the Regional Ecological Benefits category with checkboxes for connectivity, GDEs and floodplain reconnection (ID 42). Third-party wetland designation and 2015–2020 baseline water use under the MSGSA Rules (ID 40).
detail.process: Two mechanisms. (1) MLRP application: Regional Ecological Benefits is worth 25 points, assessed through checkboxes and a half-page narrative; its residual element covers ‘other benefits not quantified above’ (ID 42). No scoring formula, weighting arithmetic, scorer identity or award threshold is published. Full points can be earned for one criterion, and awards are made against an unpublished threshold (ID 45). Proposals addressing more categories score higher, and the same acreage can be claimed under several categories with no double-counting rule (ID 50). (2) MSGSA Managed Wetland Water Allocation: a habitat unit requiring third-party designation gets an entitlement quantified from a 2015–2020 baseline, with a use restriction and a duty to maintain the approved acreage. Failure triggers recalculation under Method 1 (ID 40). The ongoing test is an area test, not a function test, and the GSA performs no ecological measurement (ID 41). Opting in requires retroactive SGMA and Phase 1 fees back to FY 2019/20 (ID 57).
detail.metric: Application points and checkboxes; maintained wetland acreage; acre-foot water entitlement. Ecological condition is not measured.
detail.decision: Project selection (MLRP) and allocation eligibility (Managed Wetland). Stage: siting / implementation.
detail.gaps: No co-benefit other than water is verified after implementation. The Feasibility category is a prospective plausibility judgment (ID 44). The Managed Wetland mechanism is habitat retention rather than repurposing, because the wetland already existed in the baseline (ID 40 notes). Open: What post-implementation ecological outcome would show the claimed habitat benefit was delivered?

merced.sources: Phase 2 IDs 40, 41, 57 (MSGSA Rules & Regulations, July 2026, §2.1.2.2, p. 18 and §2.1.2.2.2.3, p. 20); 42, 44, 45, 50 (Merced MLRP RFP & Application, pp. 10, 14, 16).

salinas-valley.data: Landsat greenness, groundwater elevations, mapped GDEs; CRAM surveys
salinas-valley.process: Compute per-GDE thresholds; group sites by hydrogeology
salinas-valley.metric: GDE concern status; CRAM scores; not linked to MLRP crediting
salinas-valley.state_text: Outcome quantified, but not linked to MLRP. SVBGSA's GDE work is the most rigorous ecological accounting across the four basins. It measures the effect of groundwater depth, not of repurposing, and is not yet adopted.

detail.data: Landsat NDVI via TNC GDE Pulse; MCWRA's annual groundwater elevations; mapped potential GDEs (ID 270). California Rapid Assessment Method (CRAM) field assessments at 14 sites (ID 273).
detail.process: The 180/400 GDE Identification & Mapping report (June 2026) follows Rohde et al. (2024). For each GDE, standardized greenness (ZNDVI) is regressed on standardized depth to groundwater (ZDTG), and the threshold is computed as (ZNDVI threshold of −1 minus intercept) / slope. A GDE is ‘of concern’ in a year when ZNDVI ≤ −1 and depth exceeds the threshold (ID 270). No threshold is set where the relationship is non-significant, neutral or positive (ID 271). The method is automated in R and can be recomputed annually from two public datasets (ID 270). Reassessment is recommended on the 5-year Periodic Evaluation cycle (ID 271 notes). A second layer delineates eight GDE units by shared hydrogeology, so an impact detected in one GDE can guide monitoring of others in that unit, and adds baseline CRAM scores at 14 sites (ID 273).
detail.metric: Per-GDE depth threshold; annual ‘of concern’ status (GDEs of concern in 2015, 2021, 2022 and 2023; none in 2019, 2020 or 2024 — ID 271 notes); CRAM attribute and sub-metric scores.
detail.decision: Could guide ecosystem monitoring. It is not tied to any sustainable management criterion or management action, and the Periodic Evaluation refers only to ‘a GDE Program the SVBGSA Board will be considering in the future’ (ID 272). Stage: outcome monitoring, not linked to MLRP.
detail.gaps: The method would need to run on repurposed parcels against a counterfactual before it could act as an MLRP co-benefit metric; no document proposes this (ID 272). The GDE work and the arundo ET accounting operate on the same riparian corridor but are never combined (ID 283). CRAM limits: access could not be secured for one drought refugium, and no CRAM site exists in the Hills unit because it is oak woodland and CRAM requires wetlands (ID 273 notes). Open: What would need to change for GDE/CRAM methods to become part of MLRP monitoring?

salinas-valley.sources: Phase 2 IDs 270, 271, 272, 273 (180/400 GDE Identification & Mapping, June 2026, PDF pp. 18, 19, 28; Periodic Evaluation §2.7.2, PDF p. 79); 283 (180/400 GSP 5-Year Periodic Evaluation, Jan 2025).

literature.data: Land cover/crop type, fertilizer/N application, nitrate, pollution layers
literature.process: Estimate change in excess nitrogen / filtration opportunity
literature.metric: Excess-N reduction, nitrate/exposure risk, filtering-habitat area
literature.state_text: Outcome quantified (projected). The literature estimates water-quality change from land conversion with loading coefficients and spatial overlays. Measured concentration change at a receptor is not quantified for a specific project.

detail.data: Bryant et al. (2020): crop-specific N application rates and nitrogen-use efficiencies area-weighted by 18 SWAP crop categories, with SWRCB GAMA groundwater nitrate. Howard et al. (2023): GDE polygons, pollution-source layers and NHD surface water. Fernandez-Bou et al. (2022): DWR land use (2011–2015), nitrate loading coefficients and CDPR pesticide use reports. Dybala et al. (2025): CDPR pesticide rates (2014–2018) and Harter et al. (2017) crop-specific groundwater N loading. Supporting: Castaldo et al. (2021), geochemistry (δ¹⁸O, tritium, noble gases) from 354 domestic wells.
detail.process: (1) Excess-nitrogen change (Bryant): average annual excess N is estimated for baseline vs. retirement scenarios, then compared with existing groundwater nitrate by region. (2) Filtration overlay (Howard): GDE area lying between pollution sources and surface water within a 500 m buffer is counted as water-quality regulation. (3) Buffer coefficients (Fernandez-Bou): nitrogen-leaching and pesticide reductions are computed for land retired inside DACs and in 400 m and 1,600 m buffers; retiring 287 km² inside 156 DACs cut N leaching by an estimated 2.6 Gg/yr. (4) Land-cover loading (Dybala): per-ha pesticide and N loading × area, alternative minus baseline. (5) Recharge-source evidence (Castaldo): wells with river-water recharge signatures have significantly lower nitrate, which supports a flood-MAR water-quality pathway but gives no volume-to-concentration conversion.
detail.metric: Excess-N reduction (kg or Gg N/yr); pesticide application reduction (kg/ha/yr); area of filtering habitat; nitrate exposure risk.
detail.decision: Targets land conversion where water-quality benefit is highest. Stage: siting → projected outcome.
detail.gaps: Loading reduction is not a measured concentration change at a well or stream. Bryant found nitrate co-benefits did not align spatially with habitat priority areas. Your literature notes flag Howard's filtration measure as less defensible. Fernandez-Bou uses coefficients without a hydrologic link to specific wells. Castaldo's groundwater travel times mean benefits may take decades to appear. Open: For a claimed benefit, which contaminant, pathway and receptor should be specified?

literature.sources: Bryant et al. (2020); Howard et al. (2023); Fernandez-Bou et al. (2022); Dybala et al. (2025); Castaldo et al. (2021). Castaldo appears in your Literature Evidence sheet under DAC co-benefits and is added here as supporting evidence.

east-turlock.data: Benefit statements in GSP MA1 and three Implementation Standards
east-turlock.process: Water quality named as expected benefit; no MLRP measurement
east-turlock.state_text: Named. Water quality is listed as an expected MLRP benefit in the GSP (MA1) and as a potential benefit in three of the five Implementation Standards. No metric, monitoring requirement or verification attaches to it in any ETSGSA MLRP instrument, GSP Chapter 8, Appendix K or the WY 2025 Annual Report.

detail.data: No measurement data. The only sources are benefit statements: GSP §8.1.1.1.4 (MA1 expected benefits); the Constructed Basins, Rewilding and Stormwater Ponds Implementation Standards (p. 1 of each); and the DOC desired-outcome checkbox ‘Improved water quality’ in 2026 Application §2.2 (ID 682).
detail.process: None. The GSP quantifies MA1 only volumetrically, through C2VSimTM simulations. Its water-quality benefit is a qualitative expectation: fallowing reduces nutrient loading, and wetland habitat improves runoff quality and therefore groundwater quality (§8.1.1.1.4). The Stormwater Ponds and Constructed Basins Standards name a mechanism (sedimentation and natural filtration through vegetation, reducing downstream sediment and nutrient loads) but give no measure. The Implementation Monitoring Plan contains no water-quality term. GSP §8.2 says the GRAT siting tool is being refined to locate MLRP projects for benefits including water quality; the WY 2025 Annual Report does not report this refinement (IDs 682, 683).
detail.metric: None. The benefit is named with no constituent, concentration, load, sampling plan or threshold.
detail.decision: Applicants self-declare consistency with the DOC ‘Improved water quality’ outcome. Whether this affects scoring is unknown, because ETSGSA's scoring criteria are unpublished. Stage: application (attestation) and GSP planning expectation.
detail.gaps: Named, not measured. A logged search on 2026-10-05 covered seven water-quality terms across the 12 ETSGSA MLRP documents, GSP Chapter 8, Appendix K and the WY 2025 Annual Report, with positive controls (habitat, groundwater, MLRP). It found no MLRP water-quality metric or monitoring requirement; every Annual Report hit belongs to the Degraded Water Quality sustainability indicator (ID 683). The Earthwork Standard's SWPPP and Qualified Stormwater Professional monitoring (pp. 3–4) is construction-permit compliance, not benefit accounting. Rated Named rather than Screened because it is unknown whether the §2.2 checkbox feeds scoring. Open: Which practices are expected to change nutrient or sediment loading, and which existing monitoring network could test it?

east-turlock.sources: Phase 2 IDs 682, 683, 139. Turlock GSP 2024 §8.1.1.1.4, p. 8-10 [PDF 504]; §8.2, p. 8-55 [PDF 549]; §8.3.3.7.4 (Project 18), p. 8-123 [PDF 617]. ETSGSA Implementation Standards: Constructed Basins, Rewilding, Stormwater Ponds (p. 1 of each); Earthwork (pp. 3–4). ETSGSA MLRP 2026 Application §2.2, p. 6 [PDF 6].

kaweah.process: Use water-quality need as project rationale
kaweah.state_text: Named. Water quality is the stated purpose of one completed, community-linked recharge project. No outcome is measured.

detail.data: Public comment record on the Okieville Recharge Basin, submitted by Self-Help Enterprises (IDs 630, 631). Conditional DAC drinking-water language in the MKGSA GSP (ID 615).
detail.process: Water-quality need is the project rationale. The Okieville Recharge Basin is a 21-acre facility built in 2024 next to the Okieville DAC. TID had sought funding since 2017. Its stated purpose is wet-year recharge capacity and ‘water quality benefits to the residents of Okieville’ (ID 630). The triggering harm is quantified only in the comment record: about a quarter of the community's wells went dry in the 2012–2016 drought, and others exceeded MCLs for nitrate and arsenic (ID 631).
detail.metric: Benefit described. No constituent, concentration target, sampling plan or outcome measure.
detail.decision: Supports project rationale. Stage: siting.
detail.gaps: The recharge → wells → constituent pathway is unspecified, and no entity is assigned to monitor. The project appears in the plan record only because a commenter wrote it in (ID 630). Open: What water-quality change is expected, and who would monitor it?

kaweah.sources: Phase 2 IDs 630, 631 (Kaweah GSP Public Comments & Responses, 2024, EKGSA GSP PDF 1941, Comment column); 615 (MKGSA 2nd Amended GSP, Sec. 6.6.17.1/6.6.18.1).

merced.data: ‘Merced Water Quality and Supply’ (35 pts) + DAC water-quality criterion; spatial well layers
merced.process: Award weighted points and narrative space
merced.state_text: Screened / scored. Water-quality benefit enters through application points and narrative, with no unit of measure.

detail.data: Application rubric: the Priority category ‘Merced Water Quality and Supply (35 Points)’ (Application p. 11 [PDF 19]) and the water-quality criterion within ‘Disadvantaged Community Benefits (25 Points)’ (p. 12 [PDF 20]) (IDs 685, 687). Appendix B map of DACs (0.5-mile buffer), State Small Water Systems (1-mile buffer) and domestic-well density (ID 43).
detail.process: Applicants select criteria in ‘Merced Water Quality and Supply (35 Points)’, the highest-weighted of nine categories (170 points in total, by our sum), and write a half-page narrative (ID 684). The ‘Water Quality Benefits’ criterion asks for improvement ‘that can be measured and demonstrated’ but names no constituent, unit or method. Footnote 5 leaves the method of measurement to the applicant's narrative (ID 685). Because full points can be earned by addressing a single criterion, the 35 points can be won on supply criteria alone. Water quality is scored again under Disadvantaged Community Benefits (ID 687). Scoring is holistic against an unpublished threshold (ID 45). There is no post-implementation verification (IDs 42, 44), and stacking is rewarded with no double-counting rule (ID 50).
detail.metric: Application points and checkboxes. No water-quality unit.
detail.decision: Project selection. Stage: application.
detail.gaps: Category wording verified against Application pp. 10–12 [PDF 18–20]. The rubric requires measurable, demonstrable improvement but sets no measure and no verification step. A 35-point award does not show that any water-quality benefit was claimed. Open: When a project claims a water-quality benefit, what constituent, pathway and beneficiary should be specified up front?

merced.sources: Merced MLRP RFP p. 6 [PDF 7]; Development Project Application pp. 10–12 [PDF 18–20] and Appendix B p. 21 [PDF 29] (all within Merced_MLRP_RFP.pdf). Phase 2 IDs 42–45, 49, 50, 684, 685, 687.

salinas-valley.data: MLRP siting language names water quality & drinking-water access
salinas-valley.state_text: Screened qualitatively. Water quality is a named siting consideration and a repeatedly listed potential benefit, with no metric.

detail.data: MA2 siting language in the Periodic Evaluation (ID 257); benefit lists in the Periodic Evaluation and Response to DWR (IDs 265, 279, 280).
detail.process: Table 3-1 says water quality and access to drinking-water wells ‘will also be considered’ when deciding where to incentivize fallowing or retirement. No distance, threshold, weight or scoring rule is given (ID 257). Benefit lists name ‘water quality improvement’ and ‘improve surface water quality’ with modal verbs (‘could be’, ‘can include’) (IDs 265, 279). The Response to DWR says MLRP will ‘enhance water quality and base flow’ (ID 280), yet Table 3-2 does not credit MA2 with an ISW benefit (ID 281).
detail.metric: None. No metric or threshold.
detail.decision: Siting consideration. Stage: siting.
detail.gaps: There is a claim–instrument mismatch on base flow (IDs 280, 281). Open: Which water-quality outcome is each practice expected to affect, and which existing monitoring network could test it?

salinas-valley.sources: Phase 2 IDs 257, 265, 279, 281 (180/400 GSP 5-Year Periodic Evaluation, Jan 2025, PDF pp. 92, 111–113); 280 (SVBGSA Response to DWR, Apr 2026, PDF p. 56).

literature.data: Land cover, fallow condition, wind/soil data, receptor proximity
literature.process: Estimate dust/particulate risk vs. managed cover
literature.metric: Dust/PM reduction; acres stabilized or vegetated
literature.state_text: Named / emerging methods. Satellite attribution of dust to fallowed land and community-level risk screening exist. No field-scale protocol for a single repurposed parcel was found in the reviewed or searched literature.

detail.data: Adebiyi et al. (2025)†: USDA Cropland Data Layer fallowed-land maps (2008–2022), MODIS-derived dust optical depth, ERA5-Land meteorology, SMAP soil moisture, and IMPROVE and AERONET ground stations for validation. Ayres et al. (2022, PPIC)†: Wind Erodibility Index (WEI) soil data and baseline PM2.5 (2010–2016) around communities. Fernandez-Bou et al. (2022): names reducing particulate air contamination as a repurposing aim.
detail.process: (1) Satellite attribution (Adebiyi): major dust events are daily dust-burden anomalies more than one standard deviation above normal. The Ginoux et al. framework separates natural from anthropogenic sources, and anthropogenic event frequency is collocated with CDL fallowed parcels. (2) Community risk screen (PPIC): soils around communities are mapped with the WEI and combined with baseline PM2.5 to assign dust-risk categories (e.g., high = WEI > 86 and PM2.5 > 12 µg/m³). PPIC identifies maintaining vegetative cover as one of the easiest and most cost-effective ways to limit dust from idled land. (3) Fernandez-Bou names the air-quality benefit, but the method summary in your sheet does not describe a dust calculation.
detail.metric: Share of anthropogenic dust events associated with fallowed land (~88% in the Central Valley, which holds ~77% of California's fallowed land); dust-burden trend; community dust-risk category. A per-parcel PM10/PM2.5 or ‘acres stabilized’ metric is implied but not standardized.
detail.decision: Avoiding harmful land-idling outcomes and targeting cover requirements near exposed communities. Stage: implementation → outcome (regional).
detail.gaps: Satellite methods work at regional scale and do not verify an individual parcel. PPIC notes that long-term rural particulate monitoring is uncommon and is a knowledge gap. PPIC is a policy report, not peer-reviewed. Adebiyi also reports that fallowed areas run 4.2–8.8 °C hotter at the surface with 4.6–9.2% lower soil moisture, which is relevant if heat is added later. Open: What practical field-scale dust indicator could a GSA collect?

literature.sources: Adebiyi et al. (2025)†; Ayres, Kwon & Collins (2022, PPIC)†; Fernandez-Bou et al. (2022). † = added from outside your literature review (see References).

east-turlock.state_text: Named / safeguarded. Dust is a nuisance the landowner must avoid, not a benefit ETSGSA counts.

detail.data: Land-condition and vegetated-cover requirements in the Implementation Standards, plus visual evidence from landowner photo monitoring (IDs 142, 327).
detail.process: Word-boundary searches: ‘dust’ appears 10 times in the Implementation Standards, 0 times in GSP Chapter 8 and once in the Annual Report. Each appearance frames dust as a nuisance. Example: the Rewilding standard requires land be kept in a condition that does not create a nuisance from fire danger, dust emissions or erosion (p. 2). The only particulate reference in the MLRP corpus is ‘decreased particulate and other air emissions’, listed as an optional benefit in the Vegetated Cover standard (p. 1), with no method (ID 142). The 2026 Application lists ‘air quality benefits’ only as an optional DAC example (ID 139). Your notes record that ETSGSA documents cite CDFA Healthy Soils cover thresholds (70% orchard floor / 60% vineyard floor) (ID 622 notes).
detail.metric: No PM or dust metric.
detail.decision: Nuisance avoidance / compliance. No co-benefit credit. Stage: implementation.
detail.gaps: ETSGSA frames dust in the opposite direction from the co-benefit literature: a liability to avoid rather than a benefit to count (ID 142). Open: How is a dust problem identified in practice, and what indicator could be collected without burdensome monitoring?

east-turlock.sources: Phase 2 IDs 142 (ETSGSA MLRP Implementation Standards – Rewilding p. 2; Vegetated Cover p. 1); 139 (2026 Application §2.3.2, p. 8); 327; 622 (notes).

kaweah.process: Rule requires vegetation suppression on fallowed land
kaweah.state_text: Named / safeguarded (inverse). A binding fallowing rule requires the bare-soil condition associated with dust, and no dust provision offsets it.

detail.data: GKGSA Fifth Amended Rules & Regulations, Sec. 4.03(e) Fallowed Lands (ID 622). Dust search results across the three Kaweah GSPs (ID 623).
detail.process: To get the consumptive-use exemption for fallowing, GKGSA requires that ‘all parcels must be maintained to limit the growth of any vegetation’. The same rulebook has no dust, air-quality or ground-cover provision. The rule makes hydrologic sense, because vegetation would register ET, but the ET-ledger design gives landowners an incentive to keep repurposed land bare (ID 622). Every ‘dust’ hit across 19 pages was inspected: GPS survey boilerplate, an equipment list, and CEQA Dust Control Plan language for recharge-basin construction. Searches for PM10, fugitive and wind erosion returned 0 hits (ID 623).
detail.metric: No dust metric.
detail.decision: Land-management compliance for the ET exemption, not benefit accounting. Stage: implementation.
detail.gaps: Your notes recommend that an ET-based fallowing exemption permit or require a low-ET ground cover rather than bare soil (ID 622 notes). Open: What land condition should show that idling is not creating a dust burden?

kaweah.sources: Phase 2 IDs 622 (GKGSA Fifth Amended R&R, Mar 2026, Sec. 4.03(e), PDF 17); 623 (MKGSA 2nd Amended GSP, Sec. 6.6.6.3, PDF 362, and full-set search).

merced.process: Dust named as harm MLRP aims to avoid
merced.state_text: Named. Dust from idle fields is the harm MLRP is meant to prevent, but nothing measures it.

detail.data: RFP background language on idle-field dust; DAC scoring checkbox; Inactive Parcel/Field provisions in the MSGSA Rules §2.5.2.1 (ID 48).
detail.process: The RFP background says improperly managed idle fields ‘can emit dust and worsen air quality’, and dust appears twice more as an unmeasured DAC checkbox. The binding Inactive Parcel/Field provisions, the mechanism for idling land at scale, require only an attestation and an irrigation-absence check, with no ground-cover, revegetation or dust-management condition. A word-boundary search of the Rules returns zero hits for ‘dust’ (an earlier substring search returned 5 false hits inside ‘industrial’) (ID 48).

literature.state_text: Outcome quantified. Inundation, hydroperiod, floodplain infiltration and peak-flow attenuation all have published methods. Most of the reviewed papers quantify flood recharge rather than flood-risk reduction.

detail.data: Donnelly et al. (2023): Landsat 8/9 surface-water modeling (30 m, 2013–2022), IrrMapper and LANDFIRE. Doble et al. (2014): MODIS inundation (Open Water Likelihood), national soil and aquifer databases and bore hydrographs. Corson-Dosch et al. (2025): shallow floodplain wells, temperature probes, 0.5 m lidar and stream stage. Pakparvar et al. (2017): diversion weirs and observation wells. Bachand et al. (2014): pressure transducers, soil-moisture probes and canal flow meter. Sholtes & Doyle (2011)†: channel/valley geometry and roughness for HEC-RAS. Dybala et al. (2025): land-cover flood-tolerance scores.
detail.process: (1) Hydroperiod mapping (Donnelly): surface-water frequency classifies wetlands as temporary (<2 mo), seasonal (2–9 mo) or semi-permanent (>9 mo). (2) Flood-recharge equation (Doble 2012, 2014): actual recharge = min(potential infiltration through the clogging layer, available storage + lateral outflow), run daily on satellite inundation and validated with water-table rise × specific yield. (3) Floodplain infiltration (Corson-Dosch): four methods (head gradients, heat tracer, inundation-storage loss, vadose storage) show only 0.08–0.52% of flood volume infiltrates. (4) Diversion budget (Pakparvar): weir inflow minus outflow gives retained volume; water-table fluctuation plus a soil-water model splits flood-spreading recharge (57–61%) from rainfall. (5) On-farm capture (Bachand): check-level water-level decline minus ET gives infiltration; 15% direct and 85% in-lieu recharge. (6) Peak-flow attenuation (Sholtes & Doyle†): HEC-RAS dynamic routing compares impaired vs. restored reaches.
detail.metric: Inundated area and hydroperiod class; flood recharge volume and share of total recharge; infiltration fraction of flood volume; direct vs. in-lieu recharge split; peak-discharge attenuation.
detail.decision: Prioritizes floodplain reconnection and spreading, and verifies recharge from flood operations. Stage: siting → outcome.
detail.gaps: Inundated area overstates recharge (Corson-Dosch). The clogging-layer conductance that controls Doble's equation is hard to measure in the field. Sholtes & Doyle found that small-scale restoration gives minimal measurable attenuation, with attenuation most sensitive to slope, roughness and reach length. Donnelly is from the Intermountain West, and your notes question its transferability. Open: Which flood metric would a GSA actually use to judge success?

literature.sources: Donnelly et al. (2023); Doble et al. (2012); Doble et al. (2014); Corson-Dosch et al. (2025); Pakparvar et al. (2017); Bachand et al. (2014); Dybala et al. (2025); Sholtes & Doyle (2011)†. Your Evidence Matrix lists ‘floodplain literature’; the Doble, Corson-Dosch, Pakparvar and Bachand entries from your Literature Evidence sheet fill that reference.

literature.data: Community boundaries & vulnerability indices; land-use change
literature.process: Overlay benefits & burdens with vulnerability index
literature.state_text: Outcome quantified (projected). Frameworks allocate projected water, nitrogen, pesticide and economic changes to specific communities, weighted by vulnerability.

detail.data: Fernandez-Bou et al. (2022): DWR DAC designation (<80% statewide MHI), DWR land use, CDPR pesticide use, nitrate coefficients, SAGBI, IMPLAN and ACS. Marwaha et al. (2021): self-reported well failures, well reliance, pesticide use, InSAR subsidence and ACS poverty, linguistic-isolation and education data. Nuñez-Bolaño et al. (2025): an environmental-health risk index among six suitability layers on a 1-mile PLSS grid.
detail.process: (1) Buffer accounting (Fernandez-Bou): 156 small DACs (<15 km²) are selected; agricultural land inside each community and its 400 m and 1,600 m buffers is quantified, and groundwater-use, N-leaching and pesticide reductions plus IMPLAN revenue and employment changes are computed per buffer. (2) Vulnerability index (Marwaha): a composite of well failures, reliance, pesticides, subsidence and socio-economic factors ranks communities to prioritize recharge sites. (3) Participatory suitability (Nuñez-Bolaño): fuzzy-logic layers scaled 0–1, including environmental-health risk, are combined with stakeholder-adjustable weights in an R Shiny tool. ETSGSA's 400 m school-buffer standard cites Fernandez-Bou (ID 140).
detail.metric: Benefit by community (AF overdraft reduction, N leaching, pesticide reduction, revenue and jobs); vulnerability-weighted priority score.
detail.decision: Prioritizes projects and tests distributional equity. Stage: siting → projected outcome.
detail.gaps: All three are prospective. Fernandez-Bou uses coefficients and does not link sites to specific wells. Marwaha's index weights have no formal sensitivity analysis. Nuñez-Bolaño's weights are untested on real MLRP cases. Open: What change for residents, beyond proximity, would show a delivered community benefit?

literature.data: Domestic-well locations/depths; groundwater levels; capture zones
literature.process: Convert groundwater response/recharge into wells benefiting
literature.metric: Wells protected/failures avoided; recharge captured by community wells
literature.state_text: Outcome quantified (modeled). Published models convert groundwater-level change or recharge into failures avoided at specific domestic wells.

detail.data: Pauloo et al. (2020): 943,469 OSWCR well records, seasonal groundwater levels (1998–2017) and 2,027 reported 2012–2016 well failures. Marwaha et al. (2021): C2VSim groundwater model, OSWCR (7,673 domestic wells within 1.61 km of 288 rural communities), SAGBI and crop maps. Castaldo et al. (2021): well geochemistry.
detail.process: (1) Well-failure model (Pauloo): pump-intake depth is estimated per well, a well is ‘vulnerable’ when the kriged groundwater level comes within 3 m of the intake, and failures are projected under drought and SGMA management scenarios to 2040. (2) Capture zones (Marwaha): particle tracking in C2VSim identifies the upgradient area that recharges each domestic well, and Ag-MAR-suitable parcels inside those zones are ranked by community vulnerability. The result was 2,998 candidate parcels serving 149 communities. (3) Quality pathway (Castaldo): river-water recharge signatures are associated with lower nitrate, linking flood-MAR to long-term drinking-water quality.
detail.metric: Wells protected or failures avoided (e.g., 5,966–10,466 additional failures by 2040 under business as usual vs. 1,516–2,513 under strict sustainability, Pauloo); recharge parcels within community well capture zones.
detail.decision: Targets projects toward vulnerable drinking-water users. Stage: siting → projected outcome.
detail.gaps: Reported failures undercount actual failures. Capture zones assume steady-state flow and miss episodic flood-MAR. Pauloo does not model owners deepening wells. Castaldo's travel-time lag spans decades. Open: Which wells or systems should benefit, and how would you tell whether the project changed their outcome?

literature.data: Crop/land-use economics; farm revenue/costs; employment indicators
literature.process: Model livelihoods/economic outcomes under land-use scenarios
literature.state_text: Outcome quantified (projected). Economic models estimate opportunity cost, revenue and employment change from land-use scenarios.

detail.data: Bryant et al. (2020): SWAP agricultural economic model. Fernandez-Bou et al. (2022): IMPLAN input-output model and DWR land use. Dybala et al. (2025): CDFA crop value (2014–2020) and CEDD agricultural employment by county. Nuñez-Bolaño et al. (2025): USDA crop revenue, IMPLAN employment and DWR applied water rates.
detail.process: (1) Opportunity cost (Bryant): SWAP estimates the cultivated and retired acreage needed for SGMA compliance, and prioritizr chooses restoration that minimizes agricultural opportunity cost. (2) Input-output (Fernandez-Bou): IMPLAN estimates direct and indirect revenue and employment from repurposing DAC buffer land to clean industry or solar under low and high investment scenarios. (3) Per-ha livelihood (Dybala): gross production value and FTE jobs per ha × area by land cover, alternative minus baseline. (4) Socioeconomic index (Nuñez-Bolaño): revenue (weight 0.25), employment (0.25) and applied water (0.50), scaled 0–1, so high-water, lower-value land scores as most suitable to repurpose.
detail.metric: Opportunity cost; change in gross production value and FTE employment; spillover revenue and jobs; socioeconomic suitability score.
detail.decision: Compares strategies and compensation needs. Stage: baseline → projected outcome.
detail.gaps: All are scenario-based, not verification of realized outcomes. Bryant flags leakage when production shifts elsewhere. Fernandez-Bou's investment ranges are wide. Open: Which economic effect matters most locally — landowner income, farmworker jobs, local spending or transition cost?

literature.sources: Bryant et al. (2020); Fernandez-Bou et al. (2022); Dybala et al. (2025); Nuñez-Bolaño et al. (2025).

merced.state_text: Screened / scored. Economic resilience and job displacement are scored at application, in two categories under different framings. Transition is compensated, and outcomes are not measured.

detail.data: Application rubric: the Priority category ‘Agricultural and Economic Resiliency (25 Points)’ (Application p. 13 [PDF 21]) (ID 686) and the ‘Economic and Workforce Benefits’ criterion under Disadvantaged Community Benefits (p. 12 [PDF 20]) (ID 687). Phase 1 Land Repurposing incentive payments (ID 28).
detail.process: Applicants select among three criteria in ‘Agricultural and Economic Resiliency (25 Points)’: Supports Sustainability of Local Agriculture; Sustains Agricultural Economies (minimizing agricultural job displacement or improving pay, benefits, job security or working conditions for farmworkers); and Diversifies Economic Opportunities (ID 686). ‘Mitigation of job displacement’ is a separate criterion under Disadvantaged Community Benefits (ID 49) (ID 687). No farmworker or job-displacement measure exists in any Merced document (ID 49). Scoring is unpublished (ID 45), and outcomes are never re-checked (ID 44). Merced also runs a locally funded Phase 1 program that pays landowners under temporary 3–5 year agreements (ID 28).

detail.gaps: Wording verified against Application pp. 12–13 [PDF 20–21]. Job displacement is scored in two categories under different framings, with no measure in either, and no rule prevents one benefit being scored twice (ID 687). Row 49's note that ‘roughly a third’ of the score turns on an unmeasured construct is not supported by the 170-point arithmetic; it is under review (CLAUDE.md OQ #179). literature.data: Project access, park/trail area, proximity/population served
literature.process: Map access and observe use where feasible
literature.metric: Accessible acres, trail length, people served, visits/use
literature.state_text: Named / methods outside MLRP literature. Your review found little on recreation within MLRP. Validated access and use methods come from park and public-health research.

detail.data: Rigolon (2016)†: a review of 49 empirical park-access studies built on three parameters, proximity, acreage and quality. McKenzie et al. (2006)†: SOPARC, systematic direct observation of park users.
detail.process: (1) Access mapping (Rigolon): access is measured three ways: distance from residents to the park, park acres and acres per person, and park quality, maintenance and safety. Each is compared across socioeconomic and ethnic groups. (2) Observed use (McKenzie, SOPARC): trained observers scan defined target areas at scheduled times and count users by sex, age group, race/ethnicity and activity level, along with contextual conditions. The reliability test covered 16,244 individuals in 165 park areas, with inter-observer correlation of 0.99 for user counts.
detail.metric: Accessible acres; acres per person; distance to residents or population served; trail length; observed users and visits by group and activity.
detail.decision: Designing community-serving projects and checking whether access was delivered. Stage: siting → outcome.
detail.gaps: These methods come from urban parks and would need adapting for rural, often private, repurposed land. Rigolon found inequities mostly in acreage and quality rather than proximity, which suggests that proximity-only metrics can miss inequity. Open: If recreation is claimed, who has access, and what would be tracked?

literature.sources: Rigolon (2016)†; McKenzie et al. (2006)†. Your Evidence Matrix lists ‘relevant environmental/community-benefit literature in review’; these two sources fill that gap.
